title: Poorly Designed App
body: My review is about the app, not the device. The device may be great and very useful, but the app is poorly designed. For example, buttons and fields overlap recordings, making them difficult to access. If you only have a few recordings, you can’t scroll far enough to move them out from under those controls. Even the timestamps on the dashboard are cut off; the top row of pixels is missing from the text. The app uses icons that look AI-generated, and the overall design has that same feel. There’s nothing wrong with using AI to code, but the execution needs work. It lacks the polish I expect from an app that pairs with a $130 product, and its features feel limited compared with other recording devices and apps I’ve tested. Their desktop app is better executed than the mobile app. I also don’t see a way to organize recordings or summaries beyond a list sorted by date. There are no folders or tags that I can assign to conversations, only a search function. Even the date filter doesn’t seem to work correctly: selecting a different date changes the heading, but the recordings stay the same. For example, when I select yesterday’s date, the heading says “Yesterday,” but today’s recordings still appear at the top. Speaker identification is inconsistent, too. In a conversation between two people, the app labeled four different speakers in the transcript, while the transcript summary said “detected 2 voices.” That contradiction makes it difficult to trust the speaker labels or follow who said what. This happened in every conversation I had transcribed. One feature I really like is that the transcripts also identify background sounds, adding labels such as [keyboard clacking], [computer dings], and [toilet flushing]. It’s useful, but be aware that the app will try to identify the sounds it hears and include them in your transcript. The free membership’s limits also need to be explained more clearly. Their marketing says you get AI-generated smart summaries, but the 150-minute allowance is labeled only as “transcription minutes.” What isn’t clear is that those summaries are subject to the same limit. I understand that a free plan comes with restrictions, but the wording should make it clear that once you’ve used your 150 transcription minutes, you also stop receiving AI-generated smart summaries. If you’re trying to evaluate the device during the 14-day trial period, those 150 minutes can go quickly. You may need to pay for a month just to continue testing and decide whether the device is right for you. I did really appreciate the shipping updates built into the app. My device took quite a while to ship, but I understood there was a large backlog while they waited for devices to arrive. Being able to see when mine was being packed, shipped, and delivered right inside the app was a nice touch. You can’t get past those opening screens until you receive your device, and those screens actually look polished. Unfortunately, that level of polish doesn’t carry through to the rest of the mobile app. A UX/UI designer really needs to review this app. These are noticeable problems that make it frustrating to use.

The second infuriating aspect of this device is it does not record phone calls unless you have them on speakerphone. With a job like mine that is impossible to do even the majority of the time. The limits to their free AI subscription are such that you’re pretty much forced to pay for an upgraded subscription. If this is something you use often. title: A game changer for ADHD and follow-through
body: I almost never leave app reviews, but Fieldy has genuinely made a noticeable difference for me. I have ADHD, and one of the hardest parts of work for me isn’t doing the task — it’s remembering every little thing I said I would do, every follow-up I promised, and all of the small action items that come up naturally during conversations. Fieldy takes so much of that mental load off. I can go back and see what was discussed, turn conversations into actionable items, and keep track of commitments without feeling like I have to constantly stop and write everything down. With ADHD, sometimes I can say something and then lose the exact details surprisingly quickly, especially when I’m moving from one task to another. This gives me a reliable way to capture those moments so I can actually follow through. The biggest difference for me is that I feel more organized, more productive, and much less worried that I’m going to forget something important. It helps me keep my promises, maintain follow-ups, and stay focused on doing the work instead of using so much brainpower trying to remember the work. For me, this has been completely worth it.

body: Very highly recommend. My dad was in the hospital recently, and I was wearing my Fieldy during visits with doctors and nurses. It completely removed the pressure of trying to deeply listen, take notes, and ask questions all at once. We were able to have real conversations with the care team, knowing we could review the transcript and details later. When questions came up about what was said, we simply checked the notes and got our answers. I’ve used several AI note-taking and transcription tools for both work and personal use, and Fieldy is hands down the easiest and most effective. It’s always on, transcribes accurately, and the summaries are the best I’ve seen. This tool has been invaluable in both professional and personal situations, and I highly recommend it.
